inline.s: Mind, self-nature, intrinsic nature, Buddha-nature, the Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharma-body, consciousness, and the ālayavijñāna are all fundamental concepts in Buddhism. So that the sutras and treatises may be the better understood, they are introduced as follows.

blocks.text: 1. Self-Nature, Intrinsic Nature (the Tathāgatagarbha), and Consciousness-Nature

inline.s: Self-nature is the wondrous, luminous, all-virtuous spiritual energy; it is also called the original substance. It is this that revolves through the six realms, this that is reborn in the Pure Land of the West, and this that becomes a bodhisattva and attains Buddhahood.

[Spiritual energy] In ancient times there was no such term as “energy”; instead self-nature was called the “spiritual flame.” When the Chan master Huiji Tongzhi of Yangshan came to study with the Chan master Lingyou of Guishan, he asked:
‘Wherein does the true Buddha dwell?’
Guishan replied:

‘By the wonder of thinking without thought, turn back and contemplate the inexhaustible spiritual flame. When thought is exhausted and returns to its source, nature and appearance abide forever, and matter and principle are not two—the true Buddha remains thus, thus.’

The master (Yangshan) was instantly enlightened upon these words. (Record of the Five Lamps.) [Original substance] means self-nature. The Sixth Patriarch’s Essential Teachings on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sutra says:
“Since Bodhidharma came from the West, in order to transmit this sutra
(the Diamond Sutra)

’s meaning and cause people to awaken to principle and see their nature—only because the people of the world do not see their self-nature is the method of seeing nature established; if people were to comprehend the original substance of thusness, there would be no need to establish such a method.”
The Essential Dharma of the Mind Transmission says:
“The people of the world, not awakened, only
(ancient word used for “only”)

take seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing to be the mind, and, being covered by seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, they do not perceive the bright and essential original substance. But if one simply lets go of the mind, the original substance reveals itself of its own accord, like the great sun rising into the void, shining throughout the ten directions without the least obstruction.”

[Seeing, hearing, perceiving, knowing] is the general term for the mind’s contact with the outer world. The function of the eye-consciousness is “seeing,” of the ear-consciousness is “hearing,” of the nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses is “perceiving,” and of the mind-consciousness (the sixth consciousness) is “knowing.”
The Cultivation of the Mind says:
“The hundred bones decompose and scatter, returning to fire and wind; a single thing forever lives, covering heaven and covering earth.”
This ever-living thing is self-nature.

[The hundred bones decompose and scatter, returning to fire and wind; a single thing forever lives, covering heaven and covering earth.] The physical body rots away and returns to fire and wind (the separation of the four elements); a single thing (self-nature) forever lives, covering heaven and covering earth. [Four elements] earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has the nature of solidity, water of moisture, fire of warmth, and wind of movement. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [Hundred bones (hai)] means the various bones of a person or the whole body; here it refers to the entire body.
The Sixth Patriarch said:

“The worldly man’s physical body is a city, and the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. There are five gates without, and one gate of mind within. The mind is the ground, and one’s nature is the king, and the king dwells upon the ground of mind. When one’s nature is present the king is present; when one’s nature departs the king is gone. When one’s nature is present body and mind remain; when one’s nature departs body and mind are ruined. Seek the Buddha within one’s own nature; do not seek him outside the body. When self-nature is deluded one is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened one is a Buddha.”
(For details see
An Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Self-nature has these two states of delusion and awakening. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded one is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened one is a Buddha.”

[When self-nature is deluded one is a sentient being.] Self-nature is originally endowed with the wondrous, luminous, all-virtuous qualities, and this is Buddhahood. When self-nature is deluded, it loses those wondrous, luminous, all-virtuous qualities and falls from Buddhahood into the state of a sentient being. This is like a great magnet which, because the arrangement of its magnetic particles is disordered, loses its attractive power and becomes an ordinary lump of iron. To practice toward Buddhahood is the process by which self-nature turns from delusion to awakening, what the school calls returning to the source.
The awakening of self-nature is its original state, called intrinsic nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The Patriarch, knowing that Huineng had awakened to his intrinsic nature
(at that point the Fifth Patriarch knew that Huineng had realized his intrinsic nature)

, said to Huineng: If you do not recognize your original mind, the study of the Dharma is without benefit. If you recognize your own original mind and see your own intrinsic nature, you may be called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”

Intrinsic nature is also called Buddha-nature, the original face, and thusness. Because intrinsic nature is Buddha, it is called Buddha-nature; because it is the original state of self-nature, it is called the original face, or simply “the original”; and because it is the original state of self-nature, unchanging and forever, it is called thusness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Intrinsic nature is the Buddha; apart from nature there is no other Buddha.”
[Thusness] True means original; thus means unchanging and forever. Intrinsic nature is the original state of self-nature, forever unchanging, and therefore it is also called thusness.
To see nature is to see intrinsic nature. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“If you recognize your own original mind and see your own intrinsic nature, you may be called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”
Master Yinguang’s Groping for the Image of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi says:

“Its form is like the clouds scattering across the vast sky, the blue heavens revealed without a screen, and one sees the original face directly. Fundamentally there is nothing seen; to see without seeing is true seeing, while to have a seeing is to follow the dust.”
Intrinsic nature (Buddha-nature) is also called the Tathāgatagarbha. In the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra the Buddha says:

“The self is the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and this is my meaning. From the very beginning this meaning of mine has ever been covered by countless afflictions, and therefore sentient beings cannot see it.”
It also says:
“The true self spoken of today by the Tathāgata is called Buddha-nature.”

From this we know that the true self is Buddha-nature, that Buddha-nature is the Tathāgatagarbha, and that these are intrinsic nature. Buddha-nature and the Tathāgatagarbha are but alternate names for intrinsic nature (the true self).
The Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“The Tathāgatagarbha, intrinsically pure, transforms its thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a priceless jewel wrapped in a soiled garment.”
The Mahāyāna Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:

“The Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure, ever-lasting and never ceasing, without change, endowed with the thirty-two marks, dwelling within the bodies of all sentient beings, wrapped in the soiled garment of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, and stained by the defilements of false discrimination such as greed, hatred, and delusion—like a priceless jewel within a soiled garment.”
Master Cīen (Kuiji) says:
“The Dharma-body is originally present and shared by all Buddhas
(sharing a common identity, without distinction)
. Because ordinary beings, veiled by delusion, possess it without being aware of it, and are wrapped in afflictions, it receives the name Tathāgatagarbha.”
(The Direct Explanation of the True Mind.)

[Aggregates, elements, sense-fields] These are the five aggregates, the eighteen realms (the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses), and the twelve sense-fields (the six faculties and six objects). [Five aggregates] form, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness. [Six consciousnesses] the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousnesses. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and thinking that arise when the six faculties (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind) encounter the six objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mind-objects). [Kuiji] was the founding patriarch of the Consciousness-Only school. Because he dwelt at the Great Mercy and Kindness Monastery, he was known as Master Cīen. He was the sole son of Yuchi Gong, a meritorious minister of the early Tang; by nature he was intelligent and of imposing stature. At seventeen he submitted to the imperial edict (by imperial command) and left the home-life, becoming a foremost disciple of Master Xuanzang, from whom he studied the Buddhist sutras and treatises as well as the Indian languages. At twenty-five he took part in the translation of the scriptures. In the fourth year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong, when Master Xuanzang translated works such as the Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-Only, Kuiji alone served as the recorder, and translated the ten-fascicle Discourse on the Perfection of Consciousness-Only, and the one-fascicle Verses of the Distinguishing of the Middle and the Extremes, and the three-fascicle Discourse on the Distinguishing of the Middle and the Extremes; the one-fascicle Twenty Verses on Consciousness Only, the one-fascicle Treatise on the Schools of Different Doctrines, and the three-fascicle Treatise on the Body and Its Characteristics. Thereafter Master Xuanzang also explained for him Dignāga’s Treatise on the Correct Principle of Logic and the Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra. Thus Kuiji became versed in the science of logic and in the five-nature doctrine, and produced many commentaries, so that he was called the “master of a hundred commentaries.”
The Sutra of the Tathāgatagarbha says:
“At that time the Blessed One said to Vajraprajña and to the bodhisattvas: ...

All sentient beings, though dwelling within bodies beset by afflictions in various destinies, possess a Tathāgatagarbha that is ever undefiled, endowed with all virtuous marks, no different from me.... Therefore the Buddhas arise in the world in order to open the Dharma-treasure of the Tathāgata within their bodies, which they then believe and accept, cleansing the all-knowledge; they open the Tathāgatagarbha for all sentient beings, and with unobstructed eloquence become great givers.
Thus, good man! With the Buddha-eye I regard sentient beings as possessing the Tathāgatagarbha, and so I preach this Dharma for the bodhisattvas. At that time the Blessed One, in verse, said:
It is like a poor man’s house that holds a hidden treasure.
The owner neither knows nor sees it, and the treasure itself cannot speak.
Through the years he clings to his folly, and there is none to tell him of it.
To possess a treasure and not know it is to remain ever poor and wretched.
The Buddha-eye contemplates sentient beings who, though revolving through the five destinies,
Have the great jewel within their bodies, abiding ever without change.
Having thus observed, he preaches to sentient beings,
Enabling them to gain the treasure of wisdom, great wealth and widespread benefit.
If they believe what I say, that all possess treasure
(all sentient beings possess a precious treasure)
And with faith and diligence and skillful means, they will speedily attain the unexcelled Way.

Moreover, good man! It is like a mango whose inner kernel is not decayed; planted in the earth, it grows into a great king of trees. Thus, good man! With the Buddha-eye I regard sentient beings: the Tathāgata-treasure lies within the shell of ignorance, just as the seed of a tree lies within its kernel.... Therefore I preach the Dharma to open that Tathāgatagarbha, that they may speedily attain the unexcelled Way, as a seed becomes a king of trees
(as a fruit-seed grows into a great king of trees)

[Five destinies] Also called the five courses, they are the abodes through which sentient beings pass back and forth, and so are called destinies. They are five in number: the hell-destiny, the hungry-ghost destiny, the animal destiny, the human destiny, and the heavenly destiny.

When self-nature is deluded, it falsely takes the five aggregates’ body and mind as itself, and so, pursuing objects, it creates karma and revolves in birth and death. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says:

“What is ignorance? Good man! From time without beginning all sentient beings are subject to manifold inversions, like a man lost who takes north for south and east for west; they falsely regard the four elements’ form of their body as their own form, and the shadows of the six objects produced by the six faculties as their own mind-form. Like one whose eyes are diseased, they see flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! There are in truth no flowers in the sky; they are falsely grasped by the sick. Because of this false grasping, not only are they deluded about the nature of this empty sky, they are also deluded about the place where those flowers truly arise. From this false existence they revolve in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.”

(Translation: What is ignorance? Good man! From time without beginning all sentient beings have been subject to manifold inversions, taking the false as true—this is ignorance. This is like a man who has lost his way, taking north for south and east for west; he falsely regards the body formed from earth, water, fire, and wind as his own body-form, and the thoughts arising when the six faculties meet the six objects as his own mind-form. It is like one with diseased eyes who falsely sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! In truth there are no flowers in the sky; these are the illusions falsely grasped by the diseased eyes. Because of this false grasping, not only does one falsely hold the empty sky to be real, one also imagines that flowers truly arise there. Because sentient beings, through inversion and delusion, falsely regard these illusory body and mind as real and cling to them as self, they revolve in birth and death—and this is called ignorance.)

[Five aggregates] Form-aggregate, feeling-aggregate, perception-aggregate, volition-aggregate, and consciousness-aggregate. These five are produced by accumulation and causation, and so are called the five aggregates; and because they can cover one’s true nature, causing one to be deluded and inverted and to create various karmas, they are also called the five shrouds. Of these, the form-aggregate refers to matter and is called “form-dharmas”; the remaining four aggregates—feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness—belong to the mind and are called “mind-dharmas.” These are the five great constituents of body and mind. Of them the form-aggregate is the physical body, and the other four (feeling, perception, volition, consciousness) are the mind. [Four elements] earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has the nature of solidity, water of moisture, fire of warmth, and wind of movement. All tangible matter in the world possesses these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [Shadows of the six objects] The many thoughts produced when the six faculties meet the six objects; because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six objects—the fleeting reflections of the six objects.

The state of a deluded self-nature is called consciousness-nature; this is the deeply rooted habitual state that self-nature has developed from time without beginning by giving rise to thoughts and clinging to objects. The Cultivation of the Mind says:

“Ordinary beings, from the vast kalpas of time without beginning down to the present day, have revolved through the five destinies, dying and being born, firmly clinging to the mark of self, with false thoughts and inversions; the seeds and habits of ignorance, long accumulated, have become second nature.”
Consciousness-nature is also called the consciousness-store. Master Hanshan’s Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith says:

“The sutra says, ‘The Tathāgatagarbha transforms its thirty-two marks and enters the bodies of all sentient beings’—this is to say that the Tathāgatagarbha in its deluded state becomes the consciousness-store.”
Master Yongming Yanshou’s Record of the Mirror of the School says:
“The Tathāgatagarbha, being perfumed from time without beginning by false evil habits, is called the consciousness-store.”

Practice is the process of returning self-nature from the state of consciousness-nature (the consciousness-store) to its original state of intrinsic nature (the Tathāgatagarbha), and thereby becoming a Buddha from a sentient being.

Consciousness-nature (the consciousness-store) is also called consciousness, and is composed of eight consciousnesses: the ālayavijñāna, the manas, the mind-consciousness, and the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses. Of these, the ālayavijñāna is the fundamental consciousness, and the other seven are all derived from it. The Mahāyāna Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“The mind is born from the ālaya; the consciousnesses arise dependent on the manas; the ālaya gives rise to all the mind-states, as the ocean gives rise to waves.”

This is to say: the manas (the mind) is born from the ālayavijñāna, and the first six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) arise dependent upon the manas; therefore the first seven consciousnesses (manas, mind, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) are all derived from the ālayavijñāna. Together there are eight consciousnesses, commonly abbreviated as the eight consciousnesses. Because the first seven are derived from the ālayavijñāna, the ālayavijñāna is often used as the stand-in for consciousness-nature.
[The mind is born from the ālaya] Here “mind” means the mind-faculty among the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), that is, the manas; “ālaya” is the ālayavijñāna.
The Record of the Mirror of the School says:
“The Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says: The Tathāgatagarbha is named the ālayavijñāna, and it exists together with the seven consciousnesses of ignorance, like the waves of the great ocean, ever unceasing.”
It also says:
“The Tathāgatagarbha, being perfumed from time without beginning by false evil habits, is called the consciousness-store.”
Master Hanshan’s Notes on Observing the Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“That which is still and extinct is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.”
It also says:
“Going astray from the one mind, one becomes the eight consciousnesses.”

This is to say: when the Tathāgatagarbha (intrinsic nature) is deluded, it turns into the consciousness-store (consciousness-nature), giving rise to the eight consciousnesses—ālayavijñāna, manas, mind, eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
[One mind] The pure, single mind-substance, that is, intrinsic nature. Master Hanshan’s Notes on Observing the Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“That which is still and extinct is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.”
It also says:
“Going astray from the one mind, one becomes the eight consciousnesses.”
It also says:
“That which is called still and extinct is the one mind—that is, the intrinsically pure mind of ultimate truth, which all Buddhas have realized.”
[All Buddhas have realized this mind] This means: all Buddhas have realized this one mind (the Tathāgatagarbha).
The Sixth Patriarch, in the Platform Sutra, says:

“Self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and so is called the containing-store consciousness; if it gives rise to thinking, it is the transforming consciousness. It produces the six consciousnesses, which go out through the six gates and perceive the six objects; such are the eighteen realms, all functioning from self-nature. If self-nature is evil, the eighteen evil functions arise; if self-nature is right, the eighteen right functions arise. If the function is evil, it is the functioning of a sentient being; if good, it is the functioning of a Buddha. From what does the functioning arise? It arises from self-nature.”

(Translation: Self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and so is called the containing-store consciousness. If self-nature gives rise to thinking, this is the transforming consciousness, producing the six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). The six consciousnesses go out through the six gates (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and perceive the six objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mind-objects). Such are the eighteen realms (six consciousnesses, six gates, and six objects), all of which are self-nature functioning. If self-nature is evil, these eighteen realms function in the eighteen evil ways; if self-nature is right, they function in the eighteen right ways. If the function is evil, it is the functioning of a sentient being; if good, it is the functioning of a Buddha. From what does the function arise? From self-nature.)

In this passage the Sixth Patriarch gives an extremely important teaching on self-nature: deluded self-nature (giving rise to thinking) is consciousness (the ālayavijñāna and the other consciousnesses derived from it). It is self-nature that revolves; it is self-nature that is liberated; and it is self-nature that attains Buddhahood. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“When self-nature is deluded one is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened one is a Buddha.” “If self-nature is evil, the eighteen evil functions arise; if self-nature is right, the eighteen right functions arise. If the function is evil, it is the functioning of a sentient being; if good, it is the functioning of a Buddha.”
For a sentient being, the body is the husk, the dwelling place of self-nature (consciousness). The Platform Sutra says:
“The physical body is a dwelling place.”
Master Linji said:
“Just watch the puppet that plays upon the stage-platform; the pulling and the guiding all depend upon the one within.”
This says that the physical body is like a wooden puppet, and what manipulates it is the self-nature within. Therefore the Cultivation of the Mind says:
“The hundred bones decompose and scatter, returning to fire and wind; a single thing forever lives, covering heaven and covering earth.”

Throughout the day and the night, knowing hunger and thirst, knowing cold and heat, now angered now glad—this is self-nature. The physical body is gathered from the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; its substance is dull and without feeling. How could it see, hear, perceive, and know? That which can see, hear, perceive, and know must surely be your self-nature. A patriarch said:

“The four elements cannot understand to preach or to hear the Dharma, and the empty sky cannot understand to preach or to hear the Dharma. Only that which is before your eyes, clearly and singly alight, without form or stage ’
(that which is without form)
’, can understand to preach and to hear the Dharma. That which is without form is your self-nature.”
In terms of a single lifetime, a person’s beginning begins with self-nature (consciousness) entering the womb; a person’s end ends with self-nature (consciousness) leaving the body.
The Lalitavistara Sutra says:
“Question: What is death? Answer: To speak of death is that the consciousness departs from the body and the life-faculty has come to an end.”
The Sutra of Cause and Effect Past and Present says:

“The prince again asked: ‘What is death?’ Udayana replied: ‘That which is called death is that the knife-wind dissolves the form and the consciousness is gone, and the four limbs and all faculties know nothing more.’”
[Four limbs] refers to the whole body, the frame.
[All faculties] refers to the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Self-nature can be great and can be small:
“it universally manifests throughout all the worlds of dust, and is gathered into a single mote.”
The Sutra of the Tathāgatagarbha says:

“It is like a mango whose inner kernel is not decayed; planted in the earth, it grows into a great king of trees. Thus, good man! With the Buddha-eye I regard sentient beings: the Tathāgata-treasure lies within the shell of ignorance, just as the seed of a tree lies within its kernel.... Therefore I preach the Dharma to open that Tathāgatagarbha, that they may speedily attain the unexcelled Way, as a seed becomes a king of trees
as a fruit-seed grows into a great king of trees
Here the fruit-seed is a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha, and the great king of trees for the Dharma-body. The Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“The Tathāgatagarbha, intrinsically pure, transforms its thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a priceless jewel wrapped in a soiled garment.”
The Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith says:
“Suchness within the bonds of defilement is called the Tathāgatagarbha; suchness free of the bonds is called the Dharma-body.”
The Record of Master Mazu Daoyi says:
“Within the bonds it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; free of the bonds it is called the pure Dharma-body.”
[Worlds of dust] The world-count of the sands of the Ganges; the sands of the Ganges are used to describe a number that is vast beyond measure.

It should be noted here that, for the convenience of exposition, this article gives separate names to the deluded and the awakened states of self-nature, but in reality they are one and the same thing, just as a man’s words and deeds differ greatly when he is drunk from when he is sober, and yet it is still the same man. Therefore, in the sutras and treatises, self-nature, Buddha-nature, intrinsic nature, the true mind, and thusness are often used interchangeably. This is analyzed very clearly in the chapter “The Different Names of the True Mind” of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, which says:
“If one reaches the true mind, all its names are known; but if one is blind to the true mind, all its names become obstructions. Therefore one should be most careful about the true mind.”
(For details see
An Explanation of the Direct Explanation of the True Mind

[The simile of the drunkard] The deluded and the awakened states of self-nature, like a man’s words and deeds when drunk and when sober, differ greatly, and yet both are the doings of the same person. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:

“Blessed One, it is like a drunkard who does not know himself, does not distinguish near from far, mother from daughter, sister from sister, but wanders dazed and debauched, his speech unrestrained, lying in filth. At that time a good physician gives him a medicine to take, and having taken it, he vomits up the wine and again recalls himself, and, filled with shame, reproaches himself deeply: ‘Wine is the root of all that is not good; if I can put it away, I shall be far from all offenses.’ Blessed One, so too am I. From the past until now I have revolved in birth and death, intoxicated by passion, greedily attached to the five desires, taking as mother her who is not my mother, as sister her who is not my sister, as daughter her who is not my daughter, and taking as a sentient being those who are not sentient beings—and so I revolve, undergoing the suffering of birth and death, like that drunkard lying in filth. Let the Tathāgata now give me the medicine of the Dharma, that I may vomit up the evil wine of my afflictions.”
Question: Many sutras and treatises speak of all dharmas as without self-nature. Why does this article say that sentient beings have self-nature?

Answer: The word “self-nature” has two meanings in Buddhist studies: first, it means the wondrous, luminous, all-virtuous spiritual energy, as described above; second, it means a real substance. When it is said that “all dharmas are without self-nature,” it means that all dharmas have no real substance, being all illusions, like the affairs of a dream. Self-nature in this sense is also called natureless. The Discourse on Consciousness-Only says:
“All dharmas are without self-nature.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“Know that all dharmas are ever without nature.”
The Ūuraṃgama Sutra says:
“All illusions are without any nature.”
Question: Who is it that sees, hears, perceives, and knows? Who is it that acts, writes, speaks, and thinks? Who is it that experiences joy and anger, sorrow and delight?

Answer: All of this is self-nature. It is self-nature that, through the bodily organs, sees, hears, perceives, and knows; through the bodily organs acts, writes, speaks, and thinks; and through the bodily organs experiences joy and anger, sorrow and delight. Therefore, when the bodily organs fail, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, acting, writing, speaking, thinking, and experiencing joy and anger will correspondingly be “abnormal.” All of this is what self-nature does in its deluded state.
Question: Who becomes a sentient being? Who becomes a Buddha?
Answer: It is all self-nature. When self-nature is deluded one is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened one is a Buddha.
Question: The sutras and treatises often mention “the one mind.” What is the one mind?
Answer: “The one mind” has several meanings. First, it refers to the Tathāgatagarbha (intrinsic nature). The Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“That which is still and extinct is called the one mind, and the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.”
Second, it refers to a single thought. The Dharma Numbers of the Three Stores says:

“The one mind is the mind of a single thought. The mind-nature is all-pervading, void and transparent, numinous and penetrating; spread abroad it responds to the ten thousand things, and gathered in it becomes a single thought. Therefore, whether good or evil, sage or ordinary, everything arises from this mind. Because the mind originally possesses the ten thousand dharmas, it is able to establish all things. As the sutra says, ‘In the three realms there is no separate dharma—only this one mind creates them.’”

Third, it means this one single thought with no other thought, such as “fixing the mind on the Buddha in a single thought without scattering.” In the sutras and treatises, the case of one meaning having several names and one name having several meanings is quite common; when one encounters such a case, one must judge from the context just what is meant.
[Three realms] the desire-realm, the form-realm, and the formless realm.
Question: What is the relationship between the Dharma-body and the Tathāgatagarbha?

Answer: The Dharma-body is the true body of the Buddha, pure and tranquil, pervading the dharma-realm. In speaking earlier of intrinsic nature it was said: the intrinsic nature that has come forth from the shell of ignorance is called the Dharma-body; the intrinsic nature still within the shell of ignorance, containing and storing all the meritorious qualities of the Buddha’s fruition-ground, is called the Tathāgatagarbha. The Sutra of the Tathāgatagarbha says:

“It is like a mango whose inner kernel is not decayed; planted in the earth, it grows into a great king of trees. Thus, good man! With the Buddha-eye I regard sentient beings: the Tathāgata-treasure lies within the shell of ignorance, just as the seed of a tree lies within its kernel.... Therefore I preach the Dharma to open that Tathāgatagarbha, that they may speedily attain the unexcelled Way, as a seed becomes a king of trees
as a fruit-seed grows into a great king of trees
Here the fruit-seed is a metaphor for the Tathāgatagarbha, and the great king of trees for the Dharma-body.
The Śrīmālādevī Sutra says:
“If one does not doubt the Tathāgatagarbha wrapped in the countless store of afflictions, one will also not doubt the Dharma-body that has come forth from the countless store of afflictions.

(Those who have no doubt about the Tathāgatagarbha that is wrapped in the countless store of afflictions will also have no doubt about the Dharma-body that has come forth from that countless store of afflictions.)
.... Thus the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, never separate from the store of afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha
(the Dharma-body, never separate from the store of afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha)
The Laṃkāvatāra Sutra says:
“The Tathāgatagarbha, intrinsically pure, transforms its thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, like a priceless jewel wrapped in a soiled garment.”
The Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith says:
“Suchness
(intrinsic nature)
within the bonds of defilement is called the Tathāgatagarbha; suchness free of the bonds is called the Dharma-body.”
Master Mazu said:
“Within the bonds it is called the Tathāgatagarbha; free of the bonds it is called the pure Dharma-body.”
(The Record of Master Mazu Daoyi.)
Question: What is the relationship between the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna?

Answer: The ālayavijñāna is the eighth among the eight consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, manas, and ālayavijñāna). Because the first seven are derived from the ālayavijñāna, the ālayavijñāna is often used as a stand-in for the collection of the eight consciousnesses. In speaking of “the relationship between the Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna,” the ālayavijñāna serves as the stand-in for the collection of the eight. The Tathāgatagarbha and the ālayavijñāna are one substance in two states, just as a single piece of gold can be made into
a vase, and can also be made into a dish.
Master Zhongfeng said:
“Buddha upon Buddha is only mind; the hairpins and bracelets
(chuan, a bracelet)
, the vases and dishes, all come forth from gold.”
(Zhongfeng’s Three Sessions of Recollection.)
The ancients also used the simile of water and ice: when self-nature is in its awakened state it is the Tathāgatagarbha, just as a pool of
H
O
appears in the form of water; when in its deluded state it is the ālayavijñāna, just as
H
O
appears in the form of ice. Master Yongming said:
“Because sentient beings are deluded, they become the ālaya; because the Tathāgata is awakened, he becomes the Tathāgatagarbha.
Only when one follows the conditions of defilement does one become the deluded ālaya; when one follows the conditions of purity does one awaken and become the Tathāgatagarbha.”
(The Record of the Mirror of the School.)
Question: If a pool of
H
has part of its ice melted into water, in a state of both ice and water, does this figure the Tathāgatagarbha or the ālayavijñāna?

Answer: The state of being entirely water figures the Tathāgatagarbha; the state of being entirely ice, or of having both ice and water, figures the ālayavijñāna. The less ice there is, the higher is the degree of awakening of the ālayavijñāna.
Question: The Chan school often says,
“See the mind and realize one's nature,
see one's nature and become a Buddha.” What does this mean?
Answer:
See the mind and realize one's nature
” means:

recognize your own essential mind and see your own intrinsic nature. “Realize one's nature and become a Buddha” means: see your own intrinsic nature, and then, relying on that nature, cultivate, and perfectly realize the Buddha-way.

(“Realize one's nature and become a Buddha” does not mean that upon realizing one's nature one is immediately a Buddha.) So, “see the mind and realize one's nature; realize one's nature and become a Buddha” means: recognize your own essential mind and see your own intrinsic nature, and then, relying on that nature, cultivate, and perfectly realize the Buddha-way. (See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
Question: The Buddha taught
nonself
Yet
the Buddha
also said, at his birth,
In heaven above and earth below, I alone am the honored one.”
Is it not the case that this
is
in contradiction with “
nonself”?
[In heaven above and earth below, I alone am the honored one]
When Śākyamuni Buddha

was born, he walked seven paces toward the four directions, raised his right hand, and proclaimed: “In heaven above and earth below, I alone am the honored one; from this life onward, the share of birth is exhausted.
See Master Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions

Answer: Not at all contradictory. The “I” in the line “In heaven above and earth below, I alone am the honored one” refers to self-nature. The “I” in the word “nonself” refers to the body-and-mind of the five aggregates.
The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“All beings from beginningless time have been turned in every kind of delusion, like a lost man who wanders in every direction, mistakenly taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon.”
(See the notes in
A Detailed Explanation of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment

) This is beings in delusion, mistakenly taking the five-aggregate body and mind as self, and so the Buddha taught “nonself.” And with regard to the nonself among the “impermanent, suffering, nonself, and impure” of the śrāvaka teachings, the Buddha further taught:
“In the Buddha-dharma there is a self, which is the Buddha-nature.” “The self means the meaning of the tathāgatagarbha; all beings possess the Buddha-nature — that is the meaning of the self.”
(Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra)

To put it figuratively, the body-and-mind of the five aggregates is like a smart car, and self-nature is the owner seated inside. When one dies, it is this car that has broken down; when one is reborn, it is self-nature getting into another new car. The transmigration through the six destinies is self-nature transmigrating, and becoming a Buddha is self-nature becoming a Buddha.

The greatest trouble lies in this: in its bewilderment, self-nature mistakenly regards the body-and-mind provisionally compounded of the five aggregates as itself — self-grasping — and thereby produces karma and reaps retribution, life after life. Our practice is for self-nature to shed self-grasping and escape transmigration, no more birth, aging, sickness, and death; and further to shed dharma-grasping, and perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit.

[Self-grasping] Mistakenly clinging to the body-and-mind of the five aggregates as self. Because of self-grasping, the affliction-obstruction is formed. [Dharma-grasping] Mistakenly clinging to the path and the dharmas as real, thinking there is a dharma to be attained, a path to be cultivated, a birth-and-death to be ended, and a nirvāṇa to be realized, clinging to cultivating causes and realizing their fruits. Because of dharma-grasping, the knowledge-obstruction is formed. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
“Though the people of the two vehicles have broken the person-grasping
(that is, self-grasping)
, they still have dharma-grasping.”
The Consciousness-Only Treatise says:
“Because of self- and dharma-grasping
(because one has both self-grasping and dharma-grasping)
, the two obstructions arise together.”

[Two obstructions] The affliction-obstruction and the knowledge-obstruction. [Affliction-obstruction] The afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion that arise from mistakenly clinging to the body-and-mind of the five aggregates as self; because of the affliction-obstruction there is the birth-and-death of the intermittent body, flowing through the transmigration of the six destinies. [Knowledge-obstruction] Because of producing all kinds of erroneous views and knowledge of the path and dharmas, there is the birth-and-death of change, which obstructs the attainment of Buddhahood. [Birth-and-death of the intermittent body] In the beings of the three realms and six destinies, because of the retribution of good and evil karma, their life spans have their limits and their bodies have their sections, so their birth and death is called “the birth-and-death of the intermittent body.” One who ends the birth-and-death of the intermittent body escapes transmigration and leaves the three realms. [Birth-and-death of change] The sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thought, have ended the birth-and-death of the intermittent body. In the course of cultivation, deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually grows; this transition of delusion and awakening differs in each period. Moving from an earlier period to a later one is like a single birth and death, hence the name “birth-and-death of change.” One who ends the birth-and-death of change perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit. [Delusions of views and thought] The delusion of views and the delusion of thought. The delusion of views is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their views, such as the five false views of the view of self, the view of extremes, the false view, the view of grasping at views, and the view of clinging to precepts and practices; the delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their thoughts, such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which beings fall into the three realms and vainly undergo birth and death; cutting them off, one is able to end birth and death and leave the three realms.
“Nonself” has a deeper meaning, namely the nonself of the tathāgatagarbha; see in detail
Selected Annotations on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
the section on “the selfless tathāgatagarbha.”
Question: Is the tathāgatagarbha a real entity?

Answer: The tathāgatagarbha is not a real entity. Like all other dharmas, the tathāgatagarbha is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and is therefore an illusion. So too, self-nature, the ālayavijñāna, and the dharmakāya are all matters within the dream of ignorance — illusions. (See in detail
The Reality of All Dharmas
Question: What is the amalavijñāna?

Answer: The amalavijñāna (also written āmalavijñāna and amalavijñāna) is translated into Chinese as the undefiled consciousness, or the pure consciousness, that is, the Buddha's pure consciousness. This is the eight consciousnesses returning from the deluded causal ground to the fruit-ground of awakening. The sutra says:
“The Tathāgatas, with a single awakening, turn the various consciousnesses
(the eight consciousnesses)
, entering the amalavijñāna.”

Although the amalavijñāna too has thoughts, it is awake, supremely pure, without ignorance, and the winds of the sense-realms cannot stir it. Therefore the consciousness-nature (consciousness-store) may, according to whether or not it is defiled, be divided into two kinds: the pure undefiled consciousness and the defiled consciousness. Among the ten dharma-realms, the consciousness-nature of the Buddha is the pure consciousness; for example, when Śākyamuni Buddha expounded the teachings, though he too had thoughts, and the eight consciousnesses operated together, this was without defilement. The consciousness-natures of the other nine realms (hells, hungry ghosts, beasts, asuras, humans, gods, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas) are defiled consciousness.

[Causal ground] From the stage of ordinary beings, when one first rouses the bodhi mind to study Buddhism, up to before the perfect attainment of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the “causal ground.”
Question:
“The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharmakāya” — what does this mean? Does it come from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra? Did the Buddha say it?

Answer: The “one” in “one dharmakāya” means without difference. “One dharmakāya” means that the dharmakāyas of all Buddhas are, with one another, without difference. In Chinese, “one” is also used to mean “the same,” for example in the expression “the colors are not one.” The “one” in “one dharmakāya” means that these dharmakāyas
with one another
are without difference. “Common” means that all are thus. “
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharmakāya
” means that the dharmakāyas of all the Buddhas are,
with one another
without difference.
In none of the three Chinese translations of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra — the “Forty-roll Avataṃsaka,” the “Sixty-roll Avataṃsaka,” and the “Eighty-roll Avataṃsaka” — is there
the line “The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharmakāya.” Searching the Buddhist canon, this line is not to be found in any sutra, and indeed it was not spoken by the Buddha.
The questioner says: In the Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra
chapter ten, “The Bodhisattva Asks for Clarification,” the bodhisattva Xianshou teaches:
“The bodies of all Buddhas are but one dharmakāya, one mind, one wisdom; the powers and the fearlessness
are likewise.”
This shows that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share a single dharmakāya, and do not each have their own dharmakāya.
Answer: Here
“only one dharmakāya, one mind, one wisdom; the powers and the fearlessness are likewise”
the “one” means
with one another

without difference: the dharmakāya is without difference, and the mind, the wisdom, the powers, and the fearlessness are also without difference. This is similar in meaning to “mind, Buddha, and beings — the three are without difference.”
[Only one dharmakāya] Here the “only” (wéi) is placed at the head of the sentence and has no actual meaning.
This is a usage of classical Chinese; for example:
“Is not what Qiu sought also the affairs of a state
(Was not Ran You (Qiu) speaking of the affairs of a state?)
(The Analects
Advanced)

Mind, Buddha, and beings — the three are without difference” means: the ultimate natures of mind, Buddha, and beings are, with one another, equal, without difference. Here “mind” refers to self-nature (not the discriminating mind). And this ultimate nature is the dharmakāya. That is to say, the dharmakāyas of mind, Buddha, and beings are
with one another equal, without difference
. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra (sixty-roll version), chapter sixteen, “The Bodhisattvas of the Trayastriṃśa Heaven Speak Verses,” says:
“Mind, Buddha, and beings — these three are without difference.”
If “all Buddhas share one dharmakāya, sharing one mind, wisdom, powers, and fearlessness,” then this is in fact a single Buddha; how then can one still speak of “the Buddhas” (in the plural)?
Moreover, if “all Buddhas share one dharmakāya,” then since they share one dharmakāya, they are the same one Buddha — what need is there to add, “sharing one mind, wisdom, powers, and fearlessness”?
Moreover, the Buddha says:
My dharmakāya and the dharmakāyas of the Buddhas,
together with the marks and excellences of the form-body,
are without difference —
except that, in order to tame the beings of the various destinies who differ from one another, [I] manifest various differing form-bodies;
this is called the equality of bodies
(Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra) Here the World-Honored One (Śākyamuni Buddha) clearly teaches:
My dharmakāya and the dharmakāyas of the Buddhas,
are without difference
which is called the equality of bodies
This is plainly speaking of
the dharmakāyas of the Buddhas
being equal of body
, without difference
. Where does it say that the Buddhas share a single dharmakāya?
Moreover,
it was said earlier:
The intrinsic nature that emerges from the shell of ignorance is called the dharmakāya.
And
intrinsic nature

is the original state of self-nature. If “all Buddhas share one dharmakāya,” that is to say the Buddha and beings (beings are future Buddhas) are all one and the same self-nature. Does this make sense? Śākyamuni Buddha restored self-nature to intrinsic nature and so became a Buddha. Since we and Śākyamuni Buddha share the same self-nature, our self-nature is also restored to intrinsic nature, and we of course also become Buddhas — how then would we still be beings suffering in the evil world of the five turbidities? The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is a being; when self-nature is awakened, that is a Buddha.”
Pray tell: this single self-nature shared by the Buddha and beings — is it ultimately deluded or awakened?

From this one may know that interpreting “The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times share one dharmakāya” and “The bodies of all Buddhas are but one dharmakāya” as “all Buddhas share a single dharmakāya” is wrong.
Moreover this is a fundamental error, which leads to a mistaken understanding of the whole Buddha-dharma! Its harm is extremely great.
Question: What are the three bodies?

Answer: The three bodies are the dharmakāya, the saṃbhogakāya, and the nirmāṇakāya. The dharmakāya is also called the body of self-nature, or the body of dharma-nature; everyone originally possesses it, but we beings are deluded and do not reveal it, whereas the Buddha, being awakened, has realized it. The saṃbhogakāya is what is formed of the Buddha's wisdom and merit; it has the distinction of the saṃbhogakāya of self-enjoyment and the saṃbhogakāya of other-enjoyment. The saṃbhogakāya of self-enjoyment is the body by which the Buddha enjoys the bliss of his inner realization of the Dharma; the saṃbhogakāya of other-enjoyment is the body that the Buddha manifests to teach the Dharma to the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The nirmāṇakāya is also called the manifested body, or the transformation body, that is, the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of beings.

blocks.text: 2. Mind, Essential Mind, and Discriminating Mind

inline.s: The functioning of self-nature is called the mind. As the saying goes, “nature is the essence and mind is the function”; self-nature is the essence of the mind, and the mind is the functioning of self-nature.
The mind has two states:

1. The essential mind, that is, the original state of the mind — empty and still, without thought, numinously bright and thoroughly clear, standing alone. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“If one does not recognize the essential mind, study of the Dharma is of no benefit. If one recognizes one's own essential mind and sees one's own intrinsic nature, one is then called a great man, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.”

The essential mind is undefiled, so it is also called the pure mind. The essential mind has no knowledge yet knows everything, so the essential mind is also called the mind of numinous awareness. It should be noted: the “knowing” of the numinous awareness is the knowing of not-knowing; to distinguish it from the mark-taking knowing of seeing, hearing, and knowing, it is called numinous awareness. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowledge upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; to see and know without seeing is itself nirvāṇa, the undefiled and truly pure.”
Master Hanshan's Record on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“When the mind is still and knowing, both true and false are left behind, and this is called the self-awakened holy wisdom.”

2. The discriminating mind. The discriminating mind is also called the clinging, calculating mind — the mind that arises by grasping at the six sense-objects; it is what the Buddha in the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment called “the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects.” Its characteristic is discrimination and calculation, attachment and rejection, attraction and aversion. The stirring of thought, seeing, hearing, and knowing (here the “knowing” is the knowing of discrimination) — these are all the discriminating mind at work.

The former (the mind of numinous awareness) is awakened and is the root of nirvāṇa; the latter (the clinging, calculating mind) is deluded and is the root of birth and death. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:

“The meaning of awakening is this: the essence of the mind is free from thought. That which is free from the mark of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everything; the one mark of the dharma-realm is the Tathāgata's equal dharmakāya.”
The Chronological Autobiography of Hanshan records that Master Hanshan dreamed of going to the Tuṣita heaven and heard the bodhisattva Maitreya teach:

“Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Depending on consciousness there is defilement; depending on wisdom there is purity. Defilement involves birth and death; purity has no Buddhas.”
The Chronological Biography of Master Xuyun records that Elder Master Xuyun dreamed of going to the inner court of the Tuṣita heaven,

“where he heard the bodhisattva Maitreya lecture on the Mind-Only Concentration of Consciousness, ... and showed a verse, saying: How do consciousness and wisdom differ? They are one — the wave and the water. Do not mistake the jar and the basin; gold knows no thickness or thinness.”

(The meaning of this verse is: consciousness (the clinging, calculating mind) and wisdom (the mind of numinous awareness) are two states of one essence; consciousness is like the water of a lake when it is agitated, wisdom like the water of a lake when it is still. Using a single piece of gold to make vessels, whether one makes a jar or a basin, is only a matter of different forms. Therefore do not be deluded by their forms — in substance they have no thickness or thinness, no difference.)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, when the Fifth Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to Huineng, he said:
“If one does not recognize the essential mind, study of the Dharma is of no benefit.” Again he said, “Since ancient times, Buddhas have transmitted only the essence
(intrinsic nature)
, and from master to master have secretly handed down the essential mind.”
The founder Bodhidharma's Method of Pacifying the Mind says:

“Whatever [mind] discriminates and calculates the mind's own manifestation, all of it is a dream; if the discriminating mind is known to be quiescent and extinct, without any place of thought whatsoever, that is called right awakening.”
Practice is to quiet this scattered discriminating mind (the clinging, calculating mind) and thereby reach the state of the essential mind (the mind of numinous awareness), as the saying goes,
“If the wild mind does not rest, then when it rests, that is bodhi.”
The Essentials of Mind-Transmission says:
“When thought is stilled and deliberation forgotten, the Buddha appears before you.”
The Buddha-store Sūtra says:
“The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is without thought and without thinking.”
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“Therefore the sūtras say: If there are beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are proceeding toward the Buddha's wisdom.”
Master Hanshan, in his Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, annotates:

“This proves that non-thought is the shortcut to becoming a Buddha! The meaning is that it is not only bodhisattvas who cultivate severance [of thought] until they reach non-thought, which is called the ultimate; even among all ordinary beings, if at any time of the day and night they can contemplate non-thought, then thought after thought they move toward the Buddha's wisdom! There is no more essential resort for becoming a Buddha than this, and therefore it is specially revealed here.”
Again he says:
“All defiled dharmas arise depending on fundamental ignorance, and fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of thought. Because
(because)

beings have never in all this time been apart from thought, it is said that all defiled dharmas are the marks of non-awakening. The intent is to show that if one understands non-thought, then all afflictions are cut off at once, and therefore this points to the first thought as the root of the suffering of birth and death, wishing to make the practitioner see suffering and know its cause, and to know that leaving thought is the essential point of practice.”

[Sūtra] Here it refers to the Buddhist scriptures (sūtras). [Cultivating-severance] For good dharmas already arisen, to increase and cultivate them so that they grow; for what has not yet been attained, to be able to bring it forth. All unwholesome dharmas are then naturally cut off. This is called cultivating-severance.
Master Guifeng says:

“All dharmas are like a dream, as all the sages alike say. Therefore deluded thought is originally still, and the realms of the senses are originally empty. The empty-still mind is numinously knowing and never dim — this very empty-still awareness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind is originally self-aware; it does not arise depending on conditions, nor is it produced because of objects. The single word 'knowing'
(empty-still awareness)

is the gate of all mysteries. Because from beginningless time [beings] are deluded, they mistakenly cling to body and mind as self and give rise to thoughts of greed and hatred and so forth. If, by the instruction of a good spiritual friend, one suddenly awakens to empty-still awareness — awareness is without thought and without form, who then is the mark of self and the mark of person? Awakening to the emptiness of all marks, the mind naturally is without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; being aware, it is immediately gone. The mysterious gate of practice lies only in this. Therefore though one fully cultivates the myriad practices, one takes non-thought as the very principle. If one can attain the view and the knowing of non-thought
(that is, the knowing and seeing of non-thought)

, then love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally grow bright, offenses naturally are cut off, and merit naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are not marks, naturally there is the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are immediately severed. When arising and ceasing have ceased, still and luminous [awareness] appears before one, and its functioning is without end — this is called Buddha.”
(The General Preface to the Collected Expositions of the Source of Chan)
[The single word 'knowing' is the gate of all mysteries] Empty-still awareness is the gate of all mysteries. The Essentials of Mind-Cultivation says:
“Those who awaken to this
(empty-still awareness)
and abide in it sit in one-Thusness and attain unmoving liberation; those who are deluded about it and turn away from it go to the six destinies and transmigrate for long eons.”
(See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Essentials of Mind-Cultivation

) [Sitting in one-Thusness] “Sitting” means steadfastly maintaining. “One-Thusness”: “one” means the meaning of non-duality; “thusness” means the meaning of non-difference. Non-dual and non-different is called one-Thusness. “Sitting in one-Thusness” means steadfastly maintaining one-Thusness. As for concrete practice, it is: think of neither good nor evil, do not take up marks, abide unmoving in thusness. The Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you wish to know the essential principle of mind, simply do not think of any good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, serene and forever still, with its wondrous function as countless as the sands
(its wondrous function is endless, like the sands of the Ganges)
(See in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

) [Awakening to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, one is immediately aware; being aware, it is immediately gone. The mysterious gate of practice lies only in this] Awakening to the fact that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a deluded thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that this is taking illusion as real, being turned by illusory marks. Awakened to this point, the deluded thought also immediately disappears. The mysterious gate of practice lies right here!
[All marks are not marks] All marks whatsoever are illusions. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“Whatever has a mark is all false and vain. If one sees that all marks are not marks, one then sees the Tathāgata.”
(See the notes in
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra
Therefore, empty-still awareness is the state of the essential mind, and seeing, hearing, and knowing is the state of the discriminating mind.
The following diagram shows the two states of the mind, and the causal relationship of the thoughts of the mind.

The mind has two states: the essential mind and the discriminating mind. The essential mind is without thought; this is the state of a Buddha. The discriminating mind has thought; it is the state of beings. Among its thoughts: right thought tends toward the Buddha, deluded thought moves away from the Buddha. Good thoughts among deluded thoughts tend toward the three good destinies (gods, humans, asuras); evil thoughts tend toward the three evil destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, beasts).

[Right thought] The thought that recollects the right path. For example, the thought of Buddha-recitation of a reciter of the Buddha's name. [Deluded thought] A thought that grasps at the six sense-objects. [Tend toward] Meaning to move toward. [The essential mind is without thought] Thoughts of the mind are of three kinds: coarse thought, subtle thought, and subtlest thought. For example, for a reciter of the Buddha's name, deluded thought is coarse thought, and the thought of Buddha-recitation is subtle thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse thought and subtle thought are stilled, it is called non-thought — this is the non-thought commonly spoken of. Further, if the subtlest thought also ceases, this is the ultimate non-thought. Therefore the meaning of the word “non-thought” must be determined according to the context. The “non-thought” of “the essential mind is without thought” refers to ultimate non-thought. [Subtlest thought] The subtle arising-and-ceasing and flowing of the discriminating mind, which is the mark of the ālayavijñāna. When the subtlest thought is temporarily stilled
, self-nature presents the state of intrinsic nature — this is seeing the mind and realizing one's nature
; when the subtlest thought is forever stilled, then one perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“When the bodhisattva's stage is exhausted
(having fully cultivated the ten grounds)
, and the skillful means are fulfilled, with a single thought in accord, [one] is aware of the mind's first arising, and the mind has no first mark;
because of being far from the subtlest thought,
one sees the mind-nature
, and the mind is forever abiding,
— this is called ultimate awakening
Master Guifeng says:
“If the subtlest flowing-stream
(the subtlest thought)

is all quiescent, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone, then in response to conditions [one] manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies to deliver beings with affinity,
and this is called being a Buddha
(See the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

The process of practice is the process of stilling thought: in order, stilling coarse thought, subtle thought, and subtlest thought, so that one returns from the discriminating-mind state to the essential-mind state, returning to the original source.

The myriad thoughts returning to one is the stilling of coarse thought, leaving only subtle thought and subtlest thought. The one returning to nothing is the stilling of subtle thought, leaving only subtlest thought. Seeing the mind and realizing one's nature is the temporary stilling of the subtlest thought. Perfectly realizing the Buddha-fruit is the perpetual stilling of the subtlest thought, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone.
When self-nature is in the essential-mind state (awakened), it is intrinsic nature; when it is in the discriminating-mind state (deluded), it is consciousness-nature. The Platform Sutra says:
“When self-nature is deluded, that is a being; when self-nature is awakened, that is a Buddha.”
Again it says:
“If not awakened, then the Buddha is a being; at the moment of a single thought of awakening, a being is a Buddha.”

Take the great ocean as a simile for the mind: the state of serene stillness is the essential mind, and the state of rising waves and surging billows is the discriminating mind. The wisdom of the essential mind is prajñā; the wisdom of the discriminating mind is the wisdom of emotion (the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects). Non-thought is prajñā; thought is the wisdom of emotion. Prajñā has no knowledge yet knows everything. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
To establish knowledge upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; to see and know without seeing is itself nirvāṇa, the undefiled and truly pure.”

The essential mind is also called the true mind (here the “true” means original); the discriminating mind is also called the false mind (here the “false” is the false of false-stirring, meaning disorderly). The true mind is awakening; the false mind is delusion. Practice is to still the false and reveal the true, as the saying goes,
If the wild mind does not rest, then when it rests, that is bodhi.”

The more tranquil the water of the mind, the fainter ignorance becomes, and the more brightly prajñā shines. If the subtlest flowing-stream is forever severed, then ignorance is entirely extinguished, the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone, and this is called being a Buddha.
[Prajñā] The wisdom of the essential mind, that is, the Buddha's knowledge and insight.
The Lotus Sūtra says:

The World-Honored One appeared in the world for one great matter and one great cause-condition. What is the great matter and great cause-condition? It is, for the sake of all beings, to open up the Buddha's knowledge and insight, to show the Buddha's knowledge and insight, to cause them to awaken to the Buddha's knowledge and insight, and to enter the Buddha's knowledge and insight.
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“Prajñā-pāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas. The Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. The Dharma is precisely prajñā-pāramitā.”
The Great Prajñā Sūtra says:
“Mahāprajñā-pāramitā is the mother of all the great bodhisattvas, able to give birth to the Buddhas, and to hold and sustain the bodhisattvas.”

[Mahāprajñā-pāramitā] Translated into Chinese: the great perfection of wisdom. “Mahā” means great, and “pāramitā” means reaching the other shore. “Prajñā-pāramitā” means that prajñā is like a boat, able to ferry beings from this shore of birth and death to the other shore of nirvāṇa, which is beyond birth and death.
Master Guifeng says:
“If deluded thoughts arise and one does not follow them at all, then
(same as 'then')

at the end of life, naturally karma cannot bind; though there be an intermediate state, where one goes is free, and in the heavens or among men one may alight as one wishes. If the thoughts of love and aversion have already ceased, one no longer receives the body of intermittent birth
(no longer receives the birth and death of the intermittent body)

, and can of itself change the short for the long and the coarse for the subtle. If the subtlest flowing-stream is all quiescent, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone, then in response to conditions [one] manifests hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies to deliver beings with affinity, and this is called being a Buddha.”
(See the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
[The subtlest flowing-stream] That is, the subtlest thought — the subtle arising-and-ceasing and flowing of the discriminating mind, which is the mark of the ālayavijñāna.

Since all defiled dharmas arise depending on fundamental ignorance, and fundamental ignorance is the very first stirring of thought; therefore, if there is non-thought, all afflictions are at once cut off. Hence leaving thought is the essential point of practice! The Buddha-store Sūtra says:
“Pull up the root of all the frivolous disputations; leaving them all forever, cold and without smoke.”

From the above one may know that the endless birth and death of beings, up to their becoming Buddhas, all hang upon the one mind. Therefore practice is cultivating the mind: in order, stilling coarse thought, subtle thought, and subtlest thought.
Take the practice of Chan meditation (cānchán) as an example
(see in detail
Awareness Chan
: deluded thought is coarse thought, and the huatou (the meditation topic) is subtle thought
(right thought)
. Its process of practice is: 1. the coarse thought is stilled
(the deluded thought is stilled)
, the myriad thoughts return to one, and only the huatou remains; 2. the subtle thought is stilled
(the huatou too is gone)
, and the one returns to nothing; 3. the subtlest thought is temporarily stilled, and one sees the mind and realizes one's nature
(fully seeing the original face)
, as the saying goes, “In a single thought [delusion] at once ceases, and one fully sees intrinsic nature,” “The empty sky is shattered, and the great earth sinks flat
(vanishes)

” — this is the state at the time of the temporary stilling of the subtlest thought; 4. through maintaining [the state], the subtlest thought is forever stilled, and one perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone.
If to speak of the Pure Land school,
deluded thought is coarse thought, and the Buddha-name is subtle thought
(right thought)
. When the coarse thought is stilled
(the deluded thought is stilled)
the myriad thoughts return to one
only the Buddha-name remains
, which is single-mindedness unconfused; at the end of life, one is certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so end birth and death.
Therefore, the most direct and most incisive method of cultivation is: still the thoughts. Hence it is said:
“The mad mind does not halt; halt it and it is bodhi.”
It is also said:
“Point directly at the human mind; see one's nature and become a Buddha.”
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra
chapter on “The Arising of the Tathāgata” says:
“There is no being who does not possess the Tathāgata's wisdom, but because of false thinking, inversion, and clinging they do not realize it; if they free themselves from false thinking
(false thinking is thought: coarse thought, subtle thought, or extremely subtle thought)
, then the wisdom of all-knowing, the wisdom of spontaneity, and the unobstructed wisdom are made manifest.”
The Sūtra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
“The Buddhas' supreme, perfect enlightenment is in every case without thought and without thinking.”
The Sixth Patriarch says:

“If you wish to know the essentials of mind, simply do not deliberate on good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-essence, still and forever quiescent, yet with marvelous function as numberless as the sands of the Ganges.”
The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says:
“Still the thoughts and forget
(interchangeable with “vanquish”)
your concerns, and the Buddha appears of himself.”
On the essential mind and the intrinsic nature, the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch gives a penetrating exposition (see in detail
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

). Since the essential mind and the intrinsic nature already transcend thought and language, all words about them are merely a finger pointing at the moon; the point is that each person should follow the finger and see the moon, cultivating and awakening for himself.
Question:
“Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction”
— what does this mean?

Answer: In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, self-nature is the essence and mind is its function. In some sutras and treatises, however, the single word “mind” is used to express both the essence and the function of self-nature. Here mind is both essence and function, and “mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction” is a case of this. The sentence means: the essential nature of Buddhas and of sentient beings is in both cases self-nature, and the self-natures of all Buddhas and of all sentient beings do not differ from one another in the slightest; only their states of delusion and awakening differ. The self-nature that is perfectly awakened is a Buddha; otherwise one is a sentient being (among the ten dharma-realms, apart from the Buddha, the sentient beings of the nine realms are all called sentient beings). And among sentient beings, because the degree of delusion or awakening of each one's self-nature differs, there are the distinctions of hell-being, hungry ghost, beast, asura, human, god, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“A deluded self-nature is a sentient being; an awakened self-nature is a Buddha.”
Old Master Xuyun's Sobering Words on Chan Practice says:
“Mind is precisely the Buddha; the Buddha is precisely awakening.”
Again, Great Master Guifeng says:

“When Bodhidharma came from the west, he transmitted only the mind-dharma. Hence he said of himself: ‘My dharma transmits mind with mind and does not establish written words. This mind is the pure, original enlightenment of all sentient beings, and is also called the Buddha-nature, or the numinous awareness.
(Thus we know that the mind in “my dharma transmits mind with mind” means self-nature.)

Deluded, it gives rise to all afflictions, and afflictions too are not apart from this mind. Awakened, it gives rise to boundless marvelous function, and marvelous function too is not apart from this mind. Marvelous function and affliction, though their merit and demerit differ, and whether one is awakened or deluded, this mind is not different. To seek the Buddha-way one must awaken to this mind; hence the patriarchs of every generation transmitted only this.”
(A Chart of the Lineage and Teachers of the Chan Gate of the Transmission of Mind in China)

[The ten dharma-realms] Hell-being, hungry ghost, beast, asura, human, god, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four noble realms.
Question: What are the true mind and the false mind?

Answer: In Buddhist studies, the two terms “true mind” and “false mind” are used quite widely, and their meanings often differ. For example, some divide the eight consciousnesses into two parts, true mind and false mind: the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) is called the true mind, and the remaining seven consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, and manas) are together called the false mind. From this we can see that this is an entirely different concept from what this article says — that “the essential mind is also called the true mind (here ‘true’ means original)” and that “the consciousness-mind is also called the false mind (here ‘false’ means the false of false movement, that is, disorder).” Therefore, in reading, one must clearly know what the terms in each book mean. And a writer should likewise give clear definitions of the key terms he uses before the text begins, so that readers do not mistake one for another, so that an error of a hair's breadth does not lead a thousand miles astray, and so that pointless disputes are not stirred up, wasting precious energy and time in vain — which is a very regrettable thing.
Question:
“The whole of the true becomes the false, and the whole of the false is just the true; unchanging all day long, yet following conditions all day long”
— what does this mean?

Answer: The single thought before us has two states, the true and the false: when self-nature is master, it is true; when habitual tendencies are master, it is false. “The whole of the true becomes the false, and the whole of the false is just the true” means that the true and the false cannot both stand: either the whole is true, or the whole is false. With one deluded thought, the whole true mind turns into the false mind (the whole of the true becomes the false); with one awakened thought, the whole false mind turns into the true mind (the whole of the false is just the true). Here “true” means original: the true mind is the original state of mind. “False” means the false of false movement, that is, disorder. Because the original state is muddied and disordered by false movement, the true mind becomes the false mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“A deluded thought in the preceding moment, and one is an ordinary being; an awakened thought in the following moment, and one is a Buddha.”

Although the mind has the distinction of delusion and awakening — deluded, the whole of the true becomes the false; awakened, the whole of the false is just the true — the essence of mind (self-nature) is utterly unchanged (no arising or ceasing, no increase or decrease). This is what is meant by “unchanging all day long, yet following conditions all day long; following conditions all day long, yet unchanging all day long.”
Question: Does the essential mind (the true mind) know, or is it without knowing?
Answer: It knows. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“When knowing is established upon seeing and knowing, that is the root of ignorance.”

This shows that before ignorance arose there was originally a knowing: this is the knowing of the essential mind. This knowing is the knowing of prajñā. But the knowing that is established is the knowing of the consciousness-mind's seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing, which is the shadowy reflection of the six sense-objects.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra then says:
“When seeing and knowing are without the act of seeing, this is nirvāṇa.”
This knowing without seeing is the knowing of the essential mind.
Master Hanshan's Record of Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra says:
“When the mind is still and yet knows, and both the true and the false are transcended, this is called the noble wisdom of self-awakening.”
Master Yongjia's Yongjia Collection of the Chan School
“Śamatha Hymn, Part Four” says:
“After conditions are forgotten, all is still and still, yet the nature of numinous knowing
(the essence of mind)
is vivid and clear.”
Sengzhao's Treatise on Prajñā Being Without Knowing says:

“Because the sage's mind is without knowing, it is therefore all-knowing. The knowing of non-knowing is what is called omniscience. Hence the sutra says: ‘The sage's mind knows nothing and yet knows all.’ How true!”
Question: The single word “knowing” has long been much debated. Great Master Guifeng says:
“The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all marvels.”
Chan Master Huanglong Sixin says:
“The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all disasters.”
May I ask which of these is correct?
Answer: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“When knowing is established upon seeing and knowing, that is the root of ignorance.”
