The first “knowing” in this sentence is the gate of all marvels; but if one sinks into the second “knowing,” it is a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky, and then inviting those sky-flowers to bear sky-fruit — that is the gate of all disasters. Master Hanshan says:

“Before the Buddha appeared in the world, before the patriarch came from the west, the family estate was already complete, fully possessed by everyone. Because they possessed it yet did not know it, the Yellow-Faced One
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
and the Blue-Eyed One
(Bodhidharma)
could not help but laugh, and deliberately appeared in the world to explain it to people. The million-fold assembly at Vulture Peak and the seventeen hundred
(the seventeen hundred kōans of the Transmission of the Lamp and other records)

all turned back at a single call and instantly knew what they originally had. This is ‘the single word “knowing” is the gate of all marvels.’ Alas! The Buddhas and patriarchs originally had no substantial dharma to give people; how could they have expected that everyone would see flowers in the sky with diseased eyes, and then invite the flowers to bear fruit? Could such have been the intent of the Buddhas and patriarchs? This is ‘the single word “knowing” is the gate of all disasters.’ If we do not scrape the golden flint once more
(remove the film from the eyes, lest the diseased eye see flowers in the sky)
, how shall we inherit
(inherit and bear)
the family estate?”
(Dream-Roaming Collection
“Preface Sent to the Reverend Wuyan Dao on His Taking the Abbotship of Shaolin”) Old Man Zibai says:
“The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all marvels; when knowing is established upon seeing and knowing, the disaster is great indeed.”
(Collected Works of Old Man Zibai)
[The single word “knowing” is the gate of all marvels]
Great Master Guifeng
's Prefatory Digest of the Collected Interpretations of the Sources of Chan says:

All dharmas are like a dream — so all the sages say. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the dust-realms are originally empty. This empty and still mind, its numinous knowing is not obscured

This very knowing of empty stillness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not borrow from conditions to arise, nor does it come into being because of objects. The single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all marvels. Because from beginningless time they have been deluded, beings falsely cling to body and mind as self, and give rise to thoughts of greed, hatred, and so on. If one meets a good friend who points it out, one suddenly awakens to the knowing of empty stillness

Knowing is without thought and without form: who then is the mark of self, the mark of a person? Awakening to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, be aware of it; once aware, it is gone

and the wondrous gate of cultivation lies in this alone. Therefore, though one may cultivate all practices, one takes no-thought as the guiding principle. Once one attains the knowledge and vision of no-thought, love and aversion naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic deeds are naturally cut off, and merit naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are not marks, one naturally practices without practicing. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death come to an end
When arising and ceasing have ceased, stillness and illumination appear before one, functioning without limit — this is called a Buddha.
Therefore, “the single word ‘knowing’ is the gate of all marvels” means: the knowing of empty stillness is the gate of all marvels.

[Cannot help but laugh] Unable to keep from laughing. “Enduring the smile” means holding back laughter; “unable to stop” means having no way to control oneself. [Scraping the golden flint once more] Removing the film from the eyes, lest the diseased eye see flowers in the sky. The poem says: “The tangled film is scraped with a golden flint.” [Golden flint] An ancient tool for treating eye disease. Shaped like an arrowhead, it was used to scrape the film from the eye.
Conclusion: the knowing of empty stillness is the gate of all marvels. The knowing of discrimination is the gate of all disasters.

When the consciousness-mind engages with and reflects upon the dust-realms, the eight consciousnesses work in concert. These eight consciousnesses are: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and the ālayavijñāna. The first six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are the perceptions produced when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) engage the six dusts (dust of form, dust of sound, dust of scent, dust of flavor, dust of touch, and dust of dharma). Among these, the eye-consciousness is the perception of seeing produced when the eye-faculty engages the dust of form; the ear-consciousness is the perception of hearing produced when the ear-faculty engages the dust of sound; the nose-consciousness is the perception of smelling produced when the nose-faculty engages the dust of scent; the tongue-consciousness is the perception of tasting produced when the tongue-faculty engages the dust of flavor; the body-consciousness is the perception of touching produced when the body-faculty engages the dust of touch; and the mind-consciousness is the perception of thinking produced when the mind-faculty (manas) engages the dust of dharma. The dust of dharma is stored in the ālayavijñāna.

The process by which the consciousness-mind engages with and reflects upon the dust-realms is: feeling → perception → mental formation → consciousness. “Feeling” is the reception (perception) of the first six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) when the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, form, sound, and mind) come into contact with the six dusts (form, sound, scent, flavor, touch, and dharma). “Perception” is the thought (analysis, judgment, and synthesis) that the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) gives rise to in dependence on “feeling,” and the basis of its analysis and judgment is the relevant dust of dharma that the seventh consciousness (manas) draws out of the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna) and supplies to it. “Mental formation” is the mental activity (inner volition, such as love and hate, liking and disliking, taking up and letting go) that the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) gives rise to in dependence on “thought,” as well as the issuing of commands for action to body and speech, and so on — this is the creation of karma. “Consciousness” gathers all the information of the preceding three links, feeling, perception, and mental formation, into a comprehensive discernment (“holography”) — the karma-consciousness — which is then input through the seventh consciousness into the eighth consciousness and stored there for later use. This is what is called a karma-seed, also termed the dust of dharma, and it is what the seventh consciousness (manas) engages with.

[Karma-seeds] The karma created by sentient beings is stored in the ālayavijñāna, and because it can produce present manifestations and bear flowers and fruit, it is called a seed. Karma-seeds are also called karma-habitual tendencies, or simply seeds and habitual tendencies, and they exert a latent influence on, and even control, people's thinking and behavior.
There is a verse (the “Song of the Eight Consciousnesses”) describing the role of the eight consciousnesses in the operation of the consciousness-mind:
Eight brothers, and one of them a fool; among them one is the cleverest of all,
Five do business at the front gate, and one runs back and forth carrying news.

The one fool is the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna): it does not discriminate, does not judge, does not fabricate, and whether the information passed in is good or bad it refuses none; if something is drawn out from it, it never says “no” either — hence it is called the fool. The cleverest is the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness): it discriminates, judges, and fabricates, and is the most active. Those who do business at the front gate are the first five consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness): the eye sees form, the ear hears sound, the nose smells scent, the tongue tastes flavor, the body touches objects — they face outward objects exclusively and handle affairs. The one that runs back and forth between the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) and the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna), passing information in and out (passing in and passing out), is the seventh consciousness (manas).

Manas passes in and passes out: passing in is to knot up karma (handing the karma-consciousness to the ālayavijñāna to be stored), and passing out is to supply fuel (the dust of dharma) to the sixth consciousness so that it continues to think and deliberate. Hence the patriarch says: “If the seventh consciousness does not die, how can the dharmakāya live?” (If manas keeps on knotting up karma and grasping at the dust of dharma, how can one realize the dharmakāya?) The Treatise on the Universal Ground of the Universe says:
“Because
(owing to)

they do not comprehend the one dharma-realm, the mind does not accord with it, and suddenly a thought arises, which is named ignorance. This ignorance is also called the seventh consciousness, also called manas; it specializes in calculating and clinging to self, is the master of discrimination, and is the root of ignorance. Coming and going between the sixth and the eighth
(coming and going between the sixth consciousness and the eighth consciousness)
, passing in and passing out, it obstructs the great bright light and covers over the original.”
[One dharma-realm] The single, unique dharma-realm, that is, the reality of all dharmas. On the reality of all dharmas, see in detail
The Reality of All Dharmas

In the operation of the mind, the link of “perception” can be controlled at will, and practitioners use the “perception” of wisdom to bring about correct “mental formation,” thereby weakening and eliminating habitual tendencies. The key to turning the environment by the mind lies in working at this link of “perception” — what is called turning the thought. For example, an ordinary person hears slander and grows angry. In the Four Lessons of Liaofan, Mr. Liaofan's skill at turning the thought is this: he reflected
“There is no hero in the world who is always right, nor is there any learning that blames others
(faults others, lays blame on others)
. When one's actions do not succeed, it is always because one's own virtue is uncultivated and one's influence has not reached far. I turn it all back upon myself
(I reflect on it all in reverse)

, and then the coming of slander and abuse is a place for polishing and perfecting me; I shall gladly accept it as a gift — what anger could there be? Again, to hear slander without anger: though the flames of slander smoke the heavens, it is like holding fire to burn empty space — in the end it will go out of itself. To hear slander and grow angry: though one dispute with all one's cleverness and strength, it is like a spring silkworm spinning its cocoon, entangling itself; anger is not only useless but harmful.”

Thus he not only did not grow angry but gladly accepted it: if he had the fault, he corrected it; if not, he strove the harder. In this way he not only weakened but even uprooted the karma-seeds of having grown angry at slander in the past — this is the way to eliminate habitual tendencies.
Again, for example, Master Lianchi taught people the wondrous method of “turning the mind around and shining the light back,” which likewise begins at the link of “perception.” The Master says:
“Seventy is a rare old age; how many live to a hundred
(seventy has been rare since ancient times; how many reach a hundred?)

? At this evening scene of life, one should open one's heart wide and see through the world as no more than a play — where is there anything real? Just use one utterance of Amitābha Buddha to while away the hours, and take the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss as your home. I recite the Buddha's name now, and afterward I shall be born in the West — what fortune could be greater! Give rise to great joy and do not give rise to affliction. If you meet with something unpleasant, then at once turn your mind around: raise this one utterance of the Buddha's name urgently in mind, and shine the light back — I am a person of Amitābha Buddha's world; how could I lower myself to the level of ordinary worldly people? Turn anger into joy and recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly. This is the gate of great peace and great liberation for a person of wisdom.”
(Collected Dharmas of Yunqi)

One should check oneself at all times and in all places: am I controlled by ignorance? Have I fallen into a habitual pattern of thinking (habitual reaction)? If so, step out of it at once and let wisdom be master. In fact, resistance, discontent, criticism, anxiety, irritation, waiting, and so on are, for a practitioner, all manifestations of ignorance, tigers blocking the bodhi path, and they are also reminders that one has fallen into ignorance again. One should simply open one's heart and see through it — where is there anything real? The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch's “Hymn on the Markless” says:

“If one is truly a practitioner of the Way, one does not see the faults of the world. If one sees the faults of others, one's own fault is thereby the worse. Others' faults I do not fault; my own faults are truly mine. Just rid yourself of the fault-finding mind, and strike the afflictions down and shatter them. Hatred and love do not trouble the mind; stretch out both legs and lie at ease.”
When the mind is empty the environment is empty of itself; all dharmas bind nothing and are originally free.

Modern psychology has an ABC theory: A stands for the Activating event, B stands for Belief — the interpretation of the activating event, and C stands for the Consequence in emotion and behavior. People always hope for a good A (event) and avoid a bad A, and they strive unceasingly for this. Yet they do not know that B (the interpretation) is the one factor you can completely control and change, and that what triggers C (the consequence) is not A but B. This B (the interpretation) is precisely the link of “perception” among feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness. The same event brings joy to some families and sorrow to others. Why? Because the interpretation of the event differs (the thinking differs)! Therefore sages turn the mind and not the environment, while ordinary beings turn the environment and not the mind. So one should have the wisdom to take a step back and think, to turn the thought and think again, and to put present conditions to use for oneself. For example, suppose one is assigned the work of sweeping the ground. One kind of thinking is: why send me to do this trivial chore? — and one feels aggrieved. Turn the thought and think again: sweeping the ground is sweeping the mind; this is a splendid opportunity to test the mind in the midst of conditions — and one accepts it happily. In the process of sweeping, from the matter one arrives at the principle: outwardly sweeping away rubbish, inwardly sweeping away afflictions; and so sweeping becomes a splendid opportunity to grind away self-conceit and cultivate samādhi in the midst of movement.

The consequences of different “perceptions” are often as far apart as heaven and the abyss. After a disaster, people often sigh and, reflecting, say: what a difference one thought makes! That is precisely “perception” gone wrong.

The above explains that the “perception (thought)” of wisdom brings about correct “mental formation (mental activity),” and therefore one should constantly contemplate with wisdom. Whenever the karma-seeds of greed and hatred rise into manifestation, one should think and contemplate in accord with principle, correcting the actions of body, speech, and mind, weakening and uprooting these seeds, and replacing evil seeds with good seeds and affliction-seeds with pure seeds. Of course, if one can eliminate perception, that is all the more fierce and direct, like felling a poisonous tree by cutting straight through its root. Master Hanshan says:

“All sentient beings are deluded as to their original true mind and have always acted only in reliance on false thinking; hence in cultivation and practice, the elimination of perception is foremost.”
(A Direct Explanation of the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna)
Question: How does one weaken and uproot karma-seeds?

Answer: The crucial moment for weakening and uprooting karma-seeds is when the karma-seeds come before one; and the crucial move in weakening and uprooting them is not to give rise to a habitual reaction. The usual case is this: seeds produce present manifestations, and present manifestations perfume the seeds. That is, when a karma-seed comes before one, one gives rise to a habitual reaction (present manifestation) and creates new karma, which makes the karma-seed stored back in the ālayavijñāna stronger than before, so that when this karma-seed comes before one again it will make the habitual reaction even more intense. This is the vicious circle that makes habitual tendencies deeper and deeper (that is, makes karma-seeds stronger and stronger). Conversely, if when a karma-seed comes before one, one does not give rise to a habitual reaction but instead perceives correctly and responds wisely, then the karma-seed (habitual tendency) stored back in the ālayavijñāna is weakened, so that the next time it comes before one the habitual reaction will be weaker and easier to control. This is the virtuous circle in which present manifestation perfumes the seeds in reverse, until this karma-seed (habitual tendency) is uprooted. Therefore, when facing circumstances and meeting conditions, first stop, and with wisdom determine how one should think and how one should act, so as to cut off the habitual reaction driven by karmic force and step out of the vicious circle of delusion, karma, and suffering —
“Follow conditions to dissolve old karma, and create no new misfortune”

Therefore, if one is sunk in delusion and does not wake, then when conditions are complete there will appear the vicious circle in which the present manifestation of habitual reaction perfumes the seeds and habitual tendencies grow deeper and deeper, like constantly taking drugs, where the more one takes the greater the addiction; conversely, if one is alert at every moment, one can use the perception and mental formation of wisdom and awakening to perfume the seeds in reverse, weakening and even uprooting the original karma-seeds (habitual tendencies), like constantly breaking a drug habit, where the addiction grows smaller and smaller until it is cut off.
Knowing that the mind moves falsely and that no preceding object exists, cultivate the dharma of detachment: do not grasp, do not think.
1. Mind

blocks.text: 1. Because the mind arises, dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, dharmas cease

inline.s: [Because the mind arises, dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, dharmas cease] The mind arises (the first stirring of a thought) and one enters the dream of ignorance, and so all kinds of dharmas arise; the mind ceases (extremely subtle thoughts cease) and the dream of ignorance is awakened from, and so all kinds of dharmas cease. Therefore “the mind arises” here means the first stirring of a thought, and “the mind ceases” means the cessation of extremely subtle thoughts.
Question: “Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease” — what does this mean?
Answer: These two lines come from the
Sūtra of the Divination of the Effects of Good and Evil Karma

(see below for details). “Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise” means that the mind arises (the first stirring of a thought) and one enters the dream of ignorance, and so all kinds of dharmas appear; “because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease” means that the mind ceases (extremely subtle thoughts cease) and the dream of ignorance is awakened from, and then the all kinds of dharmas seen in the dream cease. Therefore “the mind arises” here means the first stirring of a thought (on “the first stirring of a thought,” see in detail the section below on
“the three subtle and six coarse marks”
), and “the mind ceases” means the cessation of extremely subtle thoughts. (On the dream of ignorance, see in detail
The Reality of All Dharmas

“Because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease” — this is like a person in a dream, before whom all kinds of objects appear; these objects in the dream exist in dependence on the dream-mind; when he wakes, the dream-mind no longer arises, and all the dream-scenes vanish as well. In the same way, sentient beings give rise to false thoughts (the mind arises) and enter the dream of ignorance, and so all kinds of false objects appear (hence all kinds of dharmas arise); when the false thoughts cease (the mind ceases) and the dream of ignorance is awakened from, all kinds of false objects cease (hence all kinds of dharmas cease). Moreover, not only are the objects in the dream absent when one has woken; even in the dream, did these objects ever have any reality?
The Mahāyāna Secret Adornment Sūtra says:
“As with forms in a dream
(the dust of form — that is, things that can be seen)
, which are falsely seen by thought alone and are not there once one wakes
(not there once the dream is woken from)
In the dream of ignorance
one sees the various forms of men and women and so on; when one attains perfect enlightenment
(becomes a Buddha)
, they are nowhere seen.”

[Perfect enlightenment] Becoming a Buddha is called perfect enlightenment. [When one attains perfect enlightenment, they are nowhere seen] Sentient beings, within the utterly still, unborn state, see only arising and ceasing; the Buddhas, within the manifest arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“This ignorance has no substantial entity;
like a person in a dream, who is not nonexistent while dreaming, yet when he wakes finds nothing at all

. Like flowers in the sky, which vanish into empty space, one cannot say they have a fixed place of vanishing. Why? Because they have no place of arising. All sentient beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing, and therefore it is called revolving in birth and death.”
(See the notes in detail in
A Detailed Explanation of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha to King Prasenajit on the Royal Dharma says:
“All dharmas are empty of substantial nature, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person,
in a night dream
, sees fine gardens, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, luxuriant groves and clear springs, halls and towers, all delightful; but when he awakes
(wakes from sleep)
, he sees nothing at all.”
The Sūtra of the Divination of the Effects of Good and Evil Karma says:
Again you should know that the outward aspect of mind
(the aspect of outer objects within the mind)
like the various realms seen in a dream
, is made by thought alone
(seen by the dream-mind)
, with no real outer thing. All realms are likewise: because they are all seen in reliance on the
dream of the consciousness of ignorance
, they are made by false thinking

(because false thinking causes one to enter the dream of ignorance; if there were no false thinking — if extremely subtle thoughts ceased — the dream of ignorance would be woken from and nothing would be seen)
Furthermore, you should know that because the inner mind does not abide even for a single thought
(coarse thoughts, subtle thoughts, or extremely subtle thoughts, continuing thought after thought)
, all the realms that are seen and engaged also do not abide even for a single thought, following the mind
(continuing without interruption)
— namely:
because the mind arises, all kinds of dharmas arise; because the mind ceases, all kinds of dharmas cease.
This mark of arising and ceasing
(this mark of arising and ceasing)

is merely a name and cannot really be obtained. Because the mind does not go to the realm, nor does the realm come to the mind — like an image in a mirror, which neither comes nor goes. Therefore, if one seeks a fixed mark of arising and ceasing in all dharmas, it can never be found. It is said that all dharmas are ultimately without substance, originally and always empty,
because they truly neither arise nor cease
Since all dharmas truly neither arise nor cease, there are no distinctions of any realms, but a single still flavor,
named true suchness
, the supreme meaning,
the self-nature pure mind

. That self-nature pure mind is utterly still and perfect, because it is without the mark of discrimination. Being without the mark of discrimination, it is nowhere absent. Being nowhere absent, it can support and establish all dharmas.”
That the ten realms are mind-only is shown by Master Hanshan
in
the Dream-Roaming Collection
“Instructions to Xu Qingzhi,”
where he teaches:

[The Buddha says: “The dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone.” What is above the three realms is the four noble ones beyond the world, namely Buddha, bodhisattva, śrāvaka, and pratyekabuddha. What is below the three realms is the six-destiny ordinary being: the three good destinies of god, human, and asura, and the three evil destinies of hell, beast, and hungry ghost. Thus in the ten dharma-realms, all the noble and the ordinary, the causes and effects of good and evil, and the adornments of the dependent and the principal
, are all made by the one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing other than the mind of discrimination and knowing that is present before us in our daily use.

The Buddha says: all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by one mind alone. What is above the three realms is the four noble ones beyond the world: Buddha, bodhisattva, śrāvaka, and pratyekabuddha. What is below the three realms is the six-destiny ordinary being: the three good destinies of god, human, and asura, and the three evil destinies of hell, beast, and hungry ghost. Therefore, in the ten dharma-realms, all the noble and the ordinary, the causes and effects of good and evil, and the adornments of the dependent and the principal, are entirely made by the one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing other than the mind of discrimination and knowing that is present before us in our daily use.

[The ten realms] The ten dharma-realms, namely: hell, hungry ghost, beast, asura, human, god, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four noble realms. [Dependent and principal] The dependent retribution and the principal retribution. The lands, houses, and utensils of the world, being what the body depends on, are called the “dependent retribution”; the body falsely compounded of the five aggregates, being what past karma has brought forth, is called the “principal retribution.” [Adornment] The word “adornment” here means decoration. To adorn the land with what is good and beautiful, or to adorn the body with merit and virtue, is called adornment; to pile up evil deeds upon the body is also called adornment. For example, the Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha says: “adorned with merit and virtue.” The Sūtra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Limitless Life says: “Such a foolish person steals the property of the saṅgha, robs the saṅgha of the present, teaches the dharma impurely, and has no shame or remorse, adorning himself with all kinds of evil karma.”
The Mind.

In Buddhist studies the word “mind” is used with great frequency and carries many senses; therefore one must grasp just what the “mind” spoken of in this line means. Otherwise an error of a hair's breadth will lead one a thousand miles astray. Master Hanshan states it plainly here: the “mind” by which the ten realms are mind-only,
is the very heart of our daily, immediate awareness and discriminating consciousness

The three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world where beings still bound by the two desires of lust and appetite dwell, spanning from the six heavens of desire above — through humans and animals — down to the hungry ghosts and hells. The realm of form is the world of beings who have shed the two desires of lust and appetite but still possess material bodies, comprising the four dhyānas and the eighteen heavens. The formless realm is the world of beings who, no longer having any material body, rest their mind-consciousness in deep and subtle meditative concentration, comprising the four empty heavens — the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither thinking nor not-thinking. These three realms are the sphere in which ordinary beings transmigrate through birth and death.
The dharmas above and below the three realms are all wrought by the one mind. Which

of the ten dharma-realms one is ultimately born into, together with the proper and dependent recompense one receives, is entirely wrought by the karma produced in each thought of one's own mind. Therefore the karma produced in each thought of one's own mind is the
cause
, while which dharma-realm one is born into, and what proper and dependent recompense one receives, is the
effect
. The “
wrought by the one mind
” — the “wrought” — is the making of karmic causes. As the passage below says:
“Thus among the ten dharma-realms, all sages and ordinary beings, all good and evil causes and effects,
the dependent and proper adornments
, are all created by the one mind. Yet this one mind is none other than our daily, immediate
discriminating, knowing mind
. Since all is wrought by the mind, not created step by step, but through the daily, immediate
karma wrought in each thought
it flows on through the ten dharma-realms

. If a single thought produces the ten evil deeds through greed, hatred, and delusion — the three evil acts of body, four of speech, and three of mind — that is the cause of the three miserable realms of suffering. If a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the bliss of humans and gods. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, sees no self within and no others without, and the mind is single and still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka who escapes suffering. If one observes the pleasure and pain of the present, the favorable and the adverse, arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, flowing onward and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought realizes that persons and dharmas are selfless, that causes and conditions are empty in nature, with no doer and no receiver, yet does not hinder the practice of the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, and the rest, in order to deliver living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind, originally bright and vast, containing all and saving all, with not a single dharma standing against the feelings, and living beings and Buddhas are equal, that is the cause of Buddhahood.”

Since all is wrought by the mind, not created step by step, but through the daily, immediate karma wrought in each thought, it flows on through the ten dharma-realms. If a single thought produces the ten evil deeds through greed, hatred, and delusion — the three evil acts of body, four of speech, and three of mind — that is the cause of the three miserable realms of suffering. If a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the bliss of humans and gods. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, sees no self within and no others without, and the mind is single and still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka who escapes suffering. If one observes the pleasure and pain of the present, the favorable and the adverse, arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, flowing onward and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought realizes that persons and dharmas are selfless, that causes and conditions are empty in nature, with no doer and no receiver, yet does not hinder the practice of the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, and the rest, in order to deliver living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind, originally bright and vast, containing all and saving all, with not a single dharma standing against the feelings, and living beings and Buddhas are equal, that is the cause of Buddhahood.
Though all dharmas are wrought by the mind, they are not produced in order in the wake of each thought; rather, through the karma wrought in each thought of our daily, immediate awareness
as the cause

, one receives recompense and flows through the ten dharma-realms. If a single thought produces the ten evil deeds through greed, hatred, and delusion (the three evil acts of body, four of speech, and three of mind), that is the cause of the three miserable realms of suffering. If a single thought turns the ten evil deeds into the ten good deeds, that is the cause of the bliss of humans and gods. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, sees no self within and no others without, and the mind is single and still, that is the cause of the śrāvaka who escapes suffering. If one observes the pleasure and pain of the present, the favorable and the adverse, arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, flowing onward and returning to cessation, that becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought realizes that persons and dharmas are selfless, that causes and conditions are empty in nature, with no doer and no receiver, yet does not hinder the practice of the six perfections of giving, precepts, patience, and the rest, in order to deliver living beings, that is the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind, originally bright and vast, containing all and saving all, without any differentiating perception of the feelings, and living beings and Buddhas are equal and undivided, that is the cause of Buddhahood.

The karma wrought: karma is of two kinds, common karma and individual karma. Common karma is the shared karmic cause of all beings, able to induce the world of physical forms — mountains, rivers, and the earth — that self and others enjoy together; this is the karma of the dependent recompense. Individual karma is the karmic cause by which a particular being induces its own retribution, such as differences in body, in pleasure and pain, and so forth; this is the karma of the proper recompense. Karma: all our good and evil thoughts, speech, and actions are called karma; good thought, speech, and action are called “good karma,” evil thought, speech, and action are called “evil karma.” Flowing onward and returning to cessation: producing karma and reaping the fruit of birth and death is called flowing onward; practicing the path and realizing nirvāṇa is called returning to cessation. “Returning to cessation” is returning to quiescence; that is, cultivating the path and realizing nirvāṇa.

Therefore this one mind is vast, having nothing beyond it; originally pure, perfectly full, and luminous. If in daily use, thought after thought, one awakens to this, then though one dwells amid the dust and toil, one has become a person beyond the world. This is why Vimalakīrti called it the dharma-gate of nonduality. If you, lay believer, can embody this and practice it, then all enmity and kindness, right and wrong, self and others, together with the roots of affliction and feeling, will at the touch of a thought turn into the storehouse of light. Try this in every realm encountered in daily use, and be aware thought after thought. If you cannot abide patiently, and are hindered by afflictions, then the moment you see a deluded thought arise, immediately raise the Sixth Patriarch's line “Originally not a single thing,” like the vajra king's precious sword, and all afflictions will at once melt like ice, and body and mind will turn into a cool pond. Practicing thus with vigor and never retreating, you will suddenly realize the great liberation-ground; what need then to seek the Buddha-dharma apart from this!

Therefore this one mind is vast, having nothing beyond it; originally pure, perfectly full, and luminous. If in daily use, thought after thought, one awakens to this, then though one dwells amid the dust and toil, one has become a person beyond the world. This is the dharma-gate of nonduality spoken of in the Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra. If you can embody this and practice it, then all enmity and kindness, right and wrong, self and others, together with the roots of affliction and feeling, will at the touch of a thought turn into the storehouse of light. Try this in every realm encountered in daily use, and be aware thought after thought. If you cannot abide patiently, and are hindered by afflictions, then the moment you see a deluded thought arise, immediately raise the Sixth Patriarch's line “Originally not a single thing,” like the vajra king's precious sword, and all afflictions will at once melt like ice, and body and mind will turn into a cool pond. Practicing thus with vigor and never retreating, you will suddenly realize the great liberation-ground; why then seek the Buddha-dharma apart from this!

The dharma-gate of nonduality: the teaching of the absolute, equal truth that transcends all relative distinctions. That is, above the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of Buddhism, it is the one that directly sees the holy path. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra, chapter nine, “Entering the Dharma-Gate of Nonduality,” records thirty-three such gates. Originally not a single thing: the Sixth Patriarch says, “Bodhi originally has no tree; the bright mirror is no stand. Originally not a single thing — where could dust alight?” (Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). The vajra king's precious sword: the sharp blade that cuts through all the clinging and entanglement of passion. See the Record of Linji.
A verse says:
Three dots like stars appear, one hook like the tilted moon;
Wearing fur we come from this, and become a Buddha through it too.

The first two lines of the verse depict the character “mind”; here “mind” is what was said above to be “the very heart of our daily, immediate awareness and discriminating consciousness,” that is, the single thought-mind present before us. “Wearing fur” means becoming a beast.
The Sūtra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths says:
“Because all beings differ in their thoughts, their karma too differs, and so they turn in the various destinies. O dragon king! Do you not see that in this assembly
(the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great bhikṣus, gods, humans, asuras, and others in this dharma-assembly)
and through the great sea the forms and colors of the species each differ? All of this is wrought by the mind
(nothing is not wrought by the mind)
by the good and not-good bodily karmas, verbal karmas, and mental karmas they have done.”
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
Chapter on the Ten Dedications, has a verse:
“All that exists in the world, with its many different retributions, is all brought about by the power of karma.”

Karma: all our good and evil thoughts, speech, and actions are called karma; good thought, speech, and action are called “good karma,” evil thought, speech, and action are called “evil karma.” The power of karma: the strength of karma. Good karma has the power to produce pleasurable fruits; evil karma has the power to produce painful fruits.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Five Sufferings says:

“The mind takes hell, the mind takes hungry ghosts, the mind takes beasts, the mind takes gods and humans. What fashions form and features is all the doing of the mind. He who can subdue the mind and cultivate the way has the greatest strength. I have contended with this mind for countless eons, and only now have attained Buddhahood, treading alone the three realms; all of this is the doing of the mind.”
The Sūtra on the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle says:
“The Buddhas take the Dharma as their great teacher; it is through cultivating the mind that the bodhi way is realized.”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Just use this mind, and directly awaken to Buddhahood.”
The Record of the Source Mirror says:
“Becoming a Buddha is not
(is not)
apart from this very thought.”
The ancient worthy says:
“If the wild mind does not rest, then when it rests, that is bodhi.”

blocks.text: 4. The Three Subtle and Six Coarse Markings

inline.s: Question: What is fundamental ignorance?
Answer: Fundamental ignorance (also called beginningless ignorance) is the very first stirring of thought. From this single thought arising, one
enters the dream of ignorance
, and in the long night is deluded and benighted, not understanding true principle, and so stirs delusion and produces karma. Thus
receiving retribution, one
flows through birth and death.
For a detailed account of the dream of ignorance, see the article
The Reality of All Dharmas
Question:
“One thought not awakening produces the three subtle; conditions of the field grow the six coarse.”
What does this mean?
Answer: These two lines describe the process by which intrinsic nature passes from awakening into delusion, stirring delusion
producing karma
and receiving retribution. The three subtle and the six coarse are the false aspects that intrinsic nature
enters delusion
(enters the dream of ignorance) and
illusorily
brings forth
the
nine false aspects of arising and ceasing, of flowing

: the karma-aspect of ignorance, the aspect of seeing, and the aspect of the field (the aspect of the seen); then the aspect of intellect, the aspect of continuity, the aspect of grasping, the aspect of naming, the aspect of initiating karma, and the aspect of suffering bound by karma

. Of these, the first three are produced from fundamental ignorance (“one thought not awakening produces the three subtle”); their marks are subtle, so they are called the “three subtle.” The latter six grow on the condition of the aspect of the field (“conditions of the field grow the six coarse”); their marks are coarse and manifest, so they are called the “six coarse.”
The process is
The three subtle”:
First, the karma-aspect of ignorance. The mind stirring is karma, so “not awakening, the mind stirs (the very first stirring of thought)” is called the karma-aspect of ignorance.
Second, the aspect of seeing. Depending on the foregoing “karma-aspect of ignorance,” the mind stirring then is able to see.
Third, the aspect of the field (the aspect of the seen). Depending on the foregoing “aspect of seeing,” being able to see, the field falsely manifests.
These three subtle have ignorance as their cause, so it is also said: “With ignorance as cause, the three subtle are produced.”
The six coarse”:

First, the aspect of intellect. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of the field,” one falsely gives rise to intellectual reckoning and discriminates favorable and adverse, beautiful and ugly, love and hate.
Second, the aspect of continuity. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of intellect,” in the discrimination of the field one deliberates and reckons, thought after thought in continuance.
Third, the aspect of grasping. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of continuity,” the thought of continuity deepens and gives rise to self and mine, forming the aspect of grasping.
Fourth, the aspect of naming. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of grasping,” one names the various fields, affairs, and things, forming concepts and language.
Fifth, the aspect of initiating karma. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of naming,” through deliberation and reckoning one produces various bodily, verbal, and mental karmas.

Sixth, the aspect of suffering bound by karma. Depending on the foregoing “aspect of initiating karma,” one is bound by the bodily, verbal, and mental karmas one has made and experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.
These six coarse grow on the condition of the field, so it is said: “Conditions of the field grow the six coarse.”
Among the
nine false aspects
, the first seven (
the karma-aspect of ignorance
the aspect of seeing
the aspect of the field
the aspect of intellect
the aspect of continuity
the aspect of grasping
the aspect of naming
) are delusion
the eighth (
the aspect of initiating karma
) is karma
and the ninth (
the aspect of suffering bound by karma
) is suffering
The sutra says: “Because of delusion one produces karma; because of karma one experiences suffering.” This is the process of passing from awakening into delusion.

To wake from the dream of ignorance and return from delusion to awakening is to go against the stream, to return to the source and become a Buddha: depart from suffering → do not produce karma → do not name (do not deliberate or reckon) → do not grasp (do not cling to self and mine) → sever the mind of continuity (do not have deluded thought) → do not discriminate (do not give rise to the differentiating mind of love and hate, beautiful and ugly, favorable and adverse) → extinguish coarse thought and leave the aspect of the field (do not give rise to mind toward objects — do not take up marks, abide unmoved in thusness) → extinguish subtle thought and leave the aspect of seeing → extinguish the subtle attainment and extinguish the karma-aspect of ignorance (sever fundamental ignorance and become a Buddha, waking from the dream of ignorance).

The heart of returning to the source is: leaving thought. In order, one stills the coarse thought, the subtle thought, and the subtlest thought. So the most direct and sharpest method of practice is to work at the thought-mind: still the coarse thought and the myriad thoughts return to one; still the subtle thought and the one returns to nothing; still the subtlest thought and one illumines the mind and sees nature. Then, through maintaining, deepen and consolidate the state of stilled thought until the subtlest thought is stilled forever and one becomes a Buddha.
With the coarse thought stilled, so that

“if a deluded thought arises, do not follow it (do not follow after it),” then at the end of life karma cannot bind; though there be an intermediate state, where one goes is free, and in heavens or among humans one may alight as one wishes. With the subtle thought stilled, so that “love and hate are gone,” there is no longer the birth and death of the intermittent body. With the subtlest thought stilled, one transcends the birth and death of change and becomes a Buddha, waking from the dream of ignorance.

The birth and death of the intermittent body: in the beings of the three realms and six destinies, because of the retribution of good and evil karma, their life spans have their limits and their bodies have their sections, so their birth and death is called “the birth and death of the intermittent body.” One who ends the birth and death of the intermittent body escapes transmigration and leaves the three realms. The birth and death of change: the sages of the three vehicles, having cut off the delusions of views and thought, have ended the birth and death of the intermittent body. In the course of cultivation, deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually grows; this transition of delusion and awakening differs in each period. Moving from an earlier period to a later one is like a single birth and death, hence the name “birth and death of change.” One who ends the birth and death of change fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.
Here three stages of practice are described:

First, subduing affliction (the coarse thought stilled). Its requirement is: if a deluded thought arises, do not follow it. (Please pay close attention to the word “all.”) Its effect is: at the end of life karma cannot bind; though there be an intermediate state, where one goes is free, and in heavens or among humans one may alight as one wishes.

Second, cutting off affliction (the subtle thought stilled). Its requirement is: love and hate are gone. Its effect is: ending birth and death (no more birth and death of the intermittent body), leaving the three realms (no more transmigration).

Third, realizing the Buddha-fruit (the subtlest thought stilled forever). Its requirement is: the subtlest flowing of thought all quiescent, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone. Its effect is: no more birth and death of change, appearing at will in hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies to deliver beings with affinity, and this is called being a Buddha (waking from the dream of ignorance).
Master Guifeng says:

All beings are endowed with the nature of awakening, luminous and empty, no different from the Buddha. But because from beginningless eons they have never awakened, and falsely cling to the body as self, they give rise to the feelings of love and hate and the rest. Following the feelings they produce karma; following the karma they receive retribution; in birth, aging, sickness, and death they turn for long eons. Yet the nature of awakening within the body has never known birth or death; it is like one driven in a dream while the body is at ease, or like water turned to ice while the quality of wetness is unchanged. If one could awaken to this nature
(the nature of awakening)

, it is the dharmakāya; originally unborn, what support does it need? It is spirit that is not dimmed, awareness that is always clear; it has come from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet because of the false clinging of many lives, habit has become nature, and the subtle flowing of joy, anger, sorrow, and delight continues. Though the true principle is suddenly reached, this feeling is hard to remove at once; one must be ever watchful, diminishing and diminishing again. As the wind suddenly stops and the waves gradually become still
(though the wind stops at once, the waves grow still gradually, not immediately)

, how could what is cultivated in a single life equal the power of the Buddhas? One may take emptiness and quiescence as one's own substance, not acknowledging the material body; take numinous awareness as one's own mind, not acknowledging deluded thought.
If a deluded thought arises, do not follow it
(do not follow after it)
, then at the end of life, naturally karma cannot bind
(karma naturally cannot bind)

Though there be an intermediate state, where one goes is free, and in heavens or among humans one may alight as one wishes. If love and hate are gone, one receives no longer the body of intermittent birth
(no more birth and death of the intermittent body)

, and can of itself change the short for the long and the coarse for the subtle. If the subtlest flowing of thought is all quiescent, with only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shining alone, then one appears at will in hundreds of thousands of billions of bodies to deliver beings with affinity, and this is called being a Buddha.”
(The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

Take emptiness and quiescence as one's own substance: this is spoken from a final standpoint, and so it should be when one has ended the birth and death of change. But in the stages of subduing and cutting off affliction (when ending the birth and death of the intermittent body), one should take intrinsic nature as one's own substance, so that the student has a place to begin. Numinous awareness: numinous awareness is awareness that does not take up marks; to distinguish it from the awareness of seeing, hearing, and knowing that does take up marks, it is called numinous awareness. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:
“To establish knowledge upon seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; to see and know without seeing is itself nirvāṇa, the undefiled and truly pure.”
Master Hanshan's Record on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says:
“When the mind is still and knowing, both true and false are left behind, and this is called the self-awakened holy wisdom.”

The intermediate state: the intermediate body, also called the between, is that after a person dies and before taking rebirth, a subtle material body of apparitional birth sustains life; this apparitional body is the intermediate body. In the first forty-nine days after death, this intermediate body undergoes birth and death every seven days; after seven such births and deaths, it awaits the disposition of its karmic conditions and goes to take rebirth.

Question: Beings are originally Buddhas, and with a single thought not awakening they have ignorance (fundamental ignorance), and so pass through “the three subtle and six coarse” into the cycle of birth and death. Now that we are practicing, after we become Buddhas, when will ignorance arise again and make us fall back into being sentient beings?

Answer: Our practicing now to become Buddhas is precisely to eradicate fundamental ignorance. So once fundamental ignorance is eradicated and one becomes a Buddha, ignorance will not arise again nor will one fall into being a sentient being. This is like a person who, before having smallpox, is a healthy person; having caught it, becomes a patient; after recovering, is again a healthy person, and moreover possesses lifelong immunity and will never catch smallpox again. In the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha instructs on this question, saying:
“Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it has become gold, it does not become ore again.
The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment is likewise.”
(Translation: Good man! As when smelting a gold mine, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it has been smelted into pure gold, it will not again become gold ore.
The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment (waking from the dream of ignorance) is likewise (it does not reverse).) See in detail the chapter “Three Questions on Ignorance” in the
Detailed Explanation of the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment

Fundamental ignorance: from the very beginning, a single thought not awakening, in the long night benighted and unaware of true principle, able to produce all the delusions and afflictions, is fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. The ignorance of beings and the thusness they inherently possess are both beginningless. The Sūtra on the Transcendent Practice of the Six Perfections says:

“As the wind-blown fire's fierce blaze may be checked, and the waves of the ocean may be stilled, so only the false mind is hard to subdue. Why? Because beginningless ignorance deludes the nature of the mind.”
